div.p: Long-horizon LLM agents interact with their environments through complete assistant turns while generating each action token by token. We observe that critic values vary primarily across turns, motivating optimization anchored at turns with finer credit allocation among tokens. We propose Multiscale Policy Optimization (MPO), combining Multiscale Advantage Estimation (MAE) and turn-level importance sampling to align credit assignment and policy updates at the turn scale. Extensive experiments across search, tool-use, and automation tasks with 4B and 30B-A3B models demonstrate consistent gains over strong RL baselines. Code is available at

div.head: Introduction
div.p: An LLM agent interacts with its environment through complete assistant turns, such as search queries, tool calls, and final responses, while its policy generates each turn token by token. Learning from a terminal task reward therefore involves two scale choices. Credit must connect the final outcome to interactions across the trajectory and distinguish the tokens within each interaction. Policy updates must also account for changes in complete-output probabilities while retaining those local distinctions. These choices motivate a policy-optimization method that uses both the interaction and generation scales.

Two common families of RL methods leave a gap between these scales. Critic-free, grouprelative methods, including GRPO, DAPO,and GSPO [30,44,50], derive one shared advantage per generated sequence from group-relative outcome rewards. Despite differences in their update objectives, this shared credit signal does not distinguish the contributions of individual turns or tokens within a rollout. Critic-based, token-level methods, including PPO, VC-PPO, VAPO,and SAO [9,29,45,46], use a learned value function to estimate advantages along the token sequence. Their common formulation treats each generated token as an action, providing finer credit without explicitly separating within-turn generation from turn-level environment interaction. Agentic RL therefore calls for credit assignment that captures both the contribution of each complete interaction and the relative contributions of tokens within it.

Observing credit structure across turns. Figure 2 illustrates learned values that vary within turns and exhibit larger changes across some environment interactions. Across 2,048 trajectories and 16,323 turns from eight checkpoint batches of one search-agent run, differences between turn means account for a median of 89.5% of the critic's token-weighted within-trajectory value variance. Between-turn variance exceeds within-turn variance in 93.8% of trajectories. This [5,21,44,50], as well as critic learning and long-response optimization [3,6,45,46]. Risk-based objectives further address exploration and solution diversity [12,23]. Policy optimization also targets visually grounded causal reasoning [16].

RL also supports multi-turn agents that learn through tool use and environment feedback [13,18,51]. Long horizons and sparse task rewards make credit assignment across decisions especially important [2,4,48,52]. Recent work further develops stable policy updates for asynchronous agent training [9,10]. MPO aligns advantage estimation and importance correction with complete turns, while retaining centered token-level credit within each turn.

div.head: Agentic RL Across Turns and Tokens

div.p: An LLM agent solves a task by alternating between assistant outputs and environment observations. Its interaction trajectory is 𝜏 = (𝑜 0 , 𝑎 0 , 𝑜 1 , 𝑎 1 , . . . , 𝑜 𝑇 , 𝑎 𝑇 ).

Here 𝑀 𝑡 and 𝐿 𝑡 ≥ 1 are the respective sequence lengths, and 𝑡 = 0, . . . , 𝑇 indexes assistant turns.

div.head: Policy Improvement Across Turns and Tokens
div.p: We analyze how turn-level and token-level surrogates relate to the same task-return objective. Following the surrogate-and-distribution-shift analysis of TRPO [27], we first establish a finitehorizon turn-level improvement bound, then identify the additional discrepancy introduced by token surrogates. These results motivate combining multiscale credit assignment with turn-level importance weighting in MPO. Full proofs and the extension to estimated turn advantages are provided in Appendix A.

div.p: As illustrated in Figure 1, MPO combines two components motivated by the analysis above. Its advantage estimator, MAE, propagates credit across turns and allocates it among tokens within each turn (Sections 5.1-5.2). Its policy update uses complete-turn importance weights while preserving each token's advantage in the gradient (Section 5.3).

div.head: Experimental Settings
div.p: We evaluate Qwen3-4B-Thinking and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct [22] in three agentic settings: Search, Claw-Eval, and Automation Bench. div.head: Main Results
div.p: Performance across tasks and model scales. Table 1 shows that MPO achieves the highest reported score on all nine metrics at both model sizes. Relative to the strongest non-MPO baseline in each column, MPO improves BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and HLE pass@1 by 4.33, 3.85, and 0.66 points on 4B, and by 3.59, 3.80, and 0.12 points on 30A3B. The gains extend to pass@3, including improvements of 5.11 and 5.90 points on GAIA at the two scales. MPO also improves both Claw-Eval metrics and Automation Bench performance. For example, Claw-Eval pass 3 increases by 0.95 and 1.12 points, showing that the improvements extend to success across Aligning advantage estimation and importance correction. Replacing turn-level ratios with token-level ratios reduces every reported score. The Search pass@1 drops on BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and HLE are 2.36, 3.12, and 1.03 points for 4B, and 2.05, 2.19, and 0.58 points for 30A3B. With token IS, MAE still outperforms PPO on all six Search metrics at both scales, indicating that multiscale credit assignment contributes useful gains on its own. Complete-turn importance correction provides a further improvement. Together, these comparisons support aligning shared credit and probability correction with the turn-level interaction objective, while retaining local token distinctions in the policy gradient. PPO and MPO both train the critic against terminal returns with 𝜆 critic = 1, yet MPO exhibits higher explained variance on average during late training at both model scales. A plausible explanation is that turn-aligned policy updates change the visited histories and subsequent outcomes, making their return structure easier for the critic to capture. Better value estimates may in turn improve the actor's credit signal. This interpretation concerns the interaction between policy learning and critic fitting: explained variance is measured on each policy's own rollouts and also depends on return variance, so it does not isolate a causal improvement in critic accuracy.

div.head: Test-Time Scaling
div.p: Figure 6 compares GRPO, PPO, and MPO on BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and HLE at both 4B and 30A3B scales. We report pass@k for 𝑘 ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32} using 32 independent rollouts per task, reusing the same pool for every 𝑘. All MPO curves use the full method with turn-level importance correction. Each method uses a fixed checkpoint across sampling budgets. Decoding settings, available tools, and per-rollout budgets are matched across methods.

Benefits beyond a single attempt. The gains from MPO extend to larger sampling budgets. On 4B, MPO leads GRPO and PPO at every evaluated 𝑘 on all three benchmarks. Its pass@32 reaches 75.90 on BrowseComp-Plus, 69.90 on GAIA, and 34.00 on HLE, exceeding the stronger of GRPO and PPO by 3.61, 5.82, and 5.80 points, respectively. Thus the advantage persists as additional samples expand task coverage. The 30A3B runs also benefit from additional attempts, although the relative gains depend on the benchmark and sampling budget.

These results also put the entropy curves in context. PPO's entropy drops sharply during 30A3B training while its validation performance continues to improve. Likewise, the lower entropy of 4B MPO coexists with strong performance across sampling budgets. Token entropy alone therefore does not establish a collapse in useful exploration: pass@k directly tests whether additional sampled trajectories solve tasks that a single attempt misses.

div.head: Ablation Studies
div.p: We ablate cross-turn propagation, within-turn trace length, and local refinement strength on 4B Search by varying 𝜆, 𝜆 intra , and 𝛽 one at a time. The critic target, initialization, and remaining training setup are held fixed. Tables 2 and3 report pass@1 and pass@3 on all three Search benchmarks. The reference setting is (𝜆, 𝜆 intra , 𝛽) = (0.80, 0.95, 1.00) and reproduces MPO's 4B results in Table 1. Each setting has one run. Validation learning curves for these settings appear in Appendix D.

Turn-scale propagation, 𝜆. The intermediate setting 𝜆 = 0.80 performs best among the tested values. Increasing it to 0.85 reduces BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and HLE pass@1 by 1.72, 2.21, and 1.05 points, respectively, and also reduces all three pass@3 scores. Moving closer to one thus hurts performance over this part of the tested range, consistent with a longer trace carrying more variability from distant interactions. Reducing 𝜆 to 0.60 also lowers performance, suggesting that shortening the trace too much discards useful cross-turn credit. The results favor balancing these effects rather than maximizing the propagation range.

Within-turn trace, 𝜆 intra . Reducing 𝜆 intra from 0.95 to 0.90 lowers pass@1 by 1.83, 1.55, and 1.77 points on BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and HLE, and lowers pass@3 on every benchmark. This shorter trace limits how far local TD information reaches within a generated turn. Setting 𝜆 intra = 1 also reduces all six scores relative to 0.95, including a 0.41-point drop in BrowseComp-Plus pass@1. Thus, 0.95 performs best on all six metrics in this sweep.

Different decay rates for different time scales. The two coefficients count different events: 𝜆 decays once per interaction, whereas 𝜆 intra decays once per generated token. A trajectory contains far fewer interactions than tokens, and each interaction itself requires many generated tokens. Using the same coefficient would therefore impose very different credit ranges. For example, the nominal geometric trace length 1/(1 -𝜆) is five turns at 𝜆 = 0.80, while 𝜆 intra = 0.95 gives twenty tokens; reducing the latter to 0.90 halves that local range. A smaller turn coefficient can therefore retain credit across several interactions, while a larger local coefficient avoids restricting allocation to only a few tokens. This difference motivates tuning the two scales separately and explains our choice of 𝜆 < 𝜆 intra : multiscale policy optimization uses distinct propagation ranges for environment interaction and autoregressive generation.

Local refinement strength, 𝛽. Setting 𝛽 = 0 removes within-turn credit allocation from MAE, leaving only turn-level GAE: every token in a turn receives the same turn advantage. Even without within-turn allocation, this turn-level variant outperforms the standard PPO baseline with token-level GAE in Table 1 on all six Search metrics. Its pass@1 gains over PPO are 0.95, 2.49, and 0.66 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and HLE, respectively. However, removing local allocation still substantially reduces performance relative to full MPO (Table 3). Compared with 𝛽 = 1.00, pass@1 drops by 6.28, 5.27, and 2.04 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and HLE, respectively, and pass@3 also decreases on all three benchmarks. These results show that allocating credit within a turn provides benefits beyond propagating credit across turns alone. Introducing local refinement with 𝛽 = 0.50 partially recovers the loss, while 𝛽 = 1.00 performs best on all six metrics. Increasing 𝛽 further to 1.50 and then 2.00 progressively reduces both pass@1 and pass@3 across all three benchmarks. Since the local correction is centered, these changes preserve the turn's mean advantage while amplifying differences among its tokens. The results therefore support within-turn credit allocation with a moderate refinement strength; removing it or giving it excessive weight both hurt performance.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We introduced MPO to organize LLM-agent policy optimization across turns and tokens. Its MAE component combines cross-turn credit propagation with mean-preserving local allocation, and its update aligns complete-turn importance correction with token-specific gradients. Our analysis motivates these scale choices, while experiments show gains across Search and agent tasks and continued benefits from increased sampling. The ablations support treating interaction and generation as distinct credit horizons. Together, these findings motivate using both scales when optimizing long-horizon LLM agents.

div.p: Figure 7 summarizes the original assistant-token critic predictions for all 2,048 trajectories and 16,323 turns from eight checkpoints of one MPO 4B search run.

Value differences are primarily between turns. Panel (a) compares variation around each turn's mean with variation of turn means around the trajectory mean. Most points lie above the equality line: between-turn variation exceeds within-turn variation in 93.8% of trajectories. Panel (b) shows that this pattern persists across checkpoints. The median share of variance explained by between-turn differences is 89.5% when weighting by token count and 90.2% when weighting turns equally, indicating that the pattern is not driven solely by differences in turn length.

Local token variation remains relevant. Panel (c) compares jumps from the last token value of one turn to the first of the next with the within-turn P95-P05 value span. The mean boundary jump exceeds the mean within-turn span in only 22.4% of trajectories. Panel (d) further shows that boundaries account for 9.2% of pooled squared adjacent value changes; small within-turn fluctuations accumulate over many more tokens. Thus, differences in turn-level value do not imply that most local value movement occurs at boundaries. Together, these observations motivate organizing long-range credit at the turn scale while retaining token-level refinement within each turn.
